notes.front: What is GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Copilot’s command-line interface: you use Copilot directly from your terminal to answer questions, write and debug code, and work with GitHub.com.
notes.explanation: It brings Copilot into the terminal, so you can ask it to work on code or on GitHub.com without switching tools.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: The command-line interface (CLI) for GitHub Copilot allows you to use Copilot directly from your terminal. You can use it to answer questions, write and debug code, and interact with GitHub.com.
notes.example: Like having Copilot Chat in a terminal window, but able to run commands and change files on your machine.

notes.front: In GitHub Copilot CLI, what is the interactive interface?
notes.back: A session started by entering copilot, in which you converse with Copilot, give it feedback and steer its work.
notes.explanation: Within the one conversation you can prompt Copilot to carry out one or more tasks.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Interactive interface”
notes.evidence: To start an interactive session, enter `copilot`. Within an interactive session, you can have a conversation with Copilot. You can prompt Copilot to perform one or more tasks, and you can give it feedback and steer the direction of the work.
notes.example: Like a phone call with a colleague, where you can interrupt and redirect them as they work.

notes.front: What is the programmatic interface of GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Passing the CLI a single prompt on the command line with -p or --prompt; it completes the task and then exits.
notes.explanation: To let Copilot modify and execute files this way, you also add one of the approval options.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Programmatic interface”
notes.evidence: You can also pass the CLI a single prompt directly on the command line. The CLI completes the task and then exits. To use the CLI programmatically, include the `-p` or `--prompt` command-line option in your command. To allow Copilot to modify and execute files you should also use one of the approval options
notes.example: Like sending a text message with one instruction instead of making a phone call.

notes.front: In GitHub Copilot CLI, what is a trusted directory?
notes.back: A directory in which you have allowed Copilot CLI to read, modify and execute files.
notes.explanation: Trusted directories control where the CLI may work, which is why you should only launch it from directories you trust.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Trusted directories”
notes.evidence: Trusted directories control where Copilot CLI can read, modify, and execute files. You should only launch Copilot CLI from directories that you trust.
notes.example: Like giving a builder the keys to one room of your house rather than to the whole building.

notes.front: What is compaction in GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Compressing the conversation history into a much smaller summary, freeing most of the context space for new work.
notes.explanation: Copilot keeps continuity from the summary: it knows what was discussed, what was decided and what to do next.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing context in GitHub Copilot CLI”, “What compaction does”
notes.evidence: The result is that the conversation history is compressed into a much smaller summary, freeing up the majority of the context window for new work. Copilot uses this summary to maintain continuity—it knows what was discussed, what was decided, and what to do next—even though the original messages have been replaced.
notes.example: Like replacing a long email thread with a one-page summary before carrying on the discussion.

notes.front: In GitHub Copilot CLI, what is a checkpoint?
notes.back: A saved copy of a compaction summary, stored as a numbered, titled file in the session’s workspace.
notes.explanation: One is created every time compaction happens, whether automatically or manually.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing context in GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Checkpoints”
notes.evidence: Every time compaction happens—whether automatically or manually—a **checkpoint** is created. A checkpoint is a saved copy of the compaction summary, stored as a numbered, titled file in your session's workspace.
notes.example: Like the filed minutes of each meeting in a long project, numbered in order.

notes.front: What is autopilot mode in GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: A mode in which, given full permissions, Copilot works on a task locally without stopping to prompt you for input.
notes.explanation: Your own machine does the work, and you can watch its progress in real time.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Delegating tasks to Copilot”, introduction
notes.evidence: **Autopilot mode** runs locally in your CLI session. You give autopilot full permissions and Copilot then works on a task without stopping to prompt you for input. Your local machine does the work, and you can watch progress in real time.
notes.example: Like cruise control on a motorway: the car keeps going by itself, but it is your car and you are watching.

notes.front: What does the /delegate slash command do in GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Hands the task to Copilot cloud agent on GitHub, which creates a branch, opens a draft pull request and works remotely.
notes.explanation: Because the work runs remotely, it carries on even if you shut down your local machine.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Delegating tasks to Copilot”, introduction
notes.evidence: **`/delegate`** pushes the task to Copilot cloud agent on GitHub. The work runs remotely: Copilot creates a branch, opens a draft pull request, and works in the background. Use `/delegate` when you want to hand off a task entirely and continue running even if you shut down your local machine.
notes.example: Like handing a job to a contractor who works off-site and sends back their work for your approval.

notes.back: Linux, macOS, and Windows (from PowerShell or the Windows Subsystem for Linux).

See [Copilot plans](https://github.com/features/copilot/plans?ref_product=copilot\&ref_type=engagement\&ref_style=text). * (On Windows) **PowerShell** v6 or higher If you have access to GitHub Copilot via your organization or enterprise, you cannot use Copilot CLI if your organization owner or enterprise administrator has disabled it in the organization or enterprise settings.

notes.front: On first launch, if you are not logged in to GitHub, how do you authenticate GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Enter the /login slash command and follow the on-screen instructions.
notes.explanation: The CLI itself prompts you to use this command when it finds you are not logged in.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Installing GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Authenticating with Copilot CLI”
notes.evidence: On first launch, if you're not currently logged in to GitHub, you'll be prompted to use the `/login` slash command. Enter this command and follow the on-screen instructions to authenticate.

notes.front: Which permission must a fine-grained personal access token have to authenticate GitHub Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Copilot Requests.
notes.explanation: The permission exists only on user-owned tokens, so the resource owner must be your personal account, not an organisation.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Installing GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Authenticating with a personal access token”
notes.evidence: You can also authenticate using a fine-grained personal access token with the "Copilot Requests" permission enabled. 1. Visit [Fine-grained personal access tokens](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new). 2. Under **Resource owner**, select your **personal account**. Do not select an organization. The **Copilot Requests** permission is only available on user-owned fine-grained personal access tokens.

notes.front: Of the environment variables GitHub Copilot CLI reads a token from, which takes precedence?
notes.back: `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, then `GH_TOKEN`, then `GITHUB_TOKEN`.
notes.explanation: You export the token under one of these names in your terminal or environment configuration.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Installing GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Authenticating with a personal access token”
notes.evidence: Export the token in your terminal or environment configuration. Use the `COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `GH_TOKEN`, or `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable (in order of precedence).

notes.front: Maya creates a fine-grained personal access token for Copilot CLI with her organisation as the resource owner, and cannot find the Copilot Requests permission. What should she do?
notes.back: B: create the token with her personal account as resource owner.
notes.explanation: The Copilot Requests permission is only available on user-owned fine-grained personal access tokens.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Installing GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Authenticating with a personal access token”
notes.evidence: select your **personal account**. Do not select an organization. The **Copilot Requests** permission is only available on user-owned fine-grained personal access tokens.
notes.choices:
A) Ask an organisation owner to add the permission
B) Choose her personal account as resource owner
C) Use a token with every repository permission instead
D) Skip the token: tokens cannot be used with the CLI
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: the permission does not exist on organisation-owned tokens. C is wrong: repository permissions do not replace Copilot Requests. D is wrong: a fine-grained token is a documented way to authenticate.

notes.front: While Copilot CLI is still working on a response, how can you change the direction of its work?
notes.back: Send follow-up messages to steer it, or queue instructions for it to process after its current response.
notes.explanation: This keeps you in control without waiting for Copilot to finish first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Steering the conversation”
notes.evidence: **Enqueue additional messages**: Send follow-up messages to steer the conversation in a different direction, or queue additional instructions for Copilot to process after it finishes its current response. This makes conversations feel more natural and keeps you in control.

notes.front: Besides -p, how else can you pass Copilot CLI a prompt programmatically, and which wins if you use both?
notes.back: Pipe the prompt to the copilot command; if you also give -p or --prompt, the piped input is ignored.
notes.explanation: Either way the CLI runs the prompt without an interactive session.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Running GitHub Copilot CLI programmatically”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: Pipe a prompt to the `copilot` command: ```shell copy echo "Explain this file: ./complex.ts" | copilot ``` > \[!NOTE] > Piped input is ignored if you also provide a prompt with the `-p` or `--prompt` option.

notes.front: A nightly job must ask Copilot CLI to summarise the day’s commits and then finish, with nobody at the keyboard. Which interface fits?
notes.back: B: the programmatic interface, passing the prompt with -p.
notes.explanation: Given a single prompt on the command line, the CLI completes the task and then exits.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Programmatic interface”
notes.evidence: You can also pass the CLI a single prompt directly on the command line. The CLI completes the task and then exits.
notes.choices:
A) The interactive interface, started with copilot
B) The programmatic interface, with -p
C) /delegate from an interactive session
D) Plan mode
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: an interactive session waits for a person to converse with it. C is wrong: /delegate hands work to Copilot cloud agent, which opens a pull request. D is wrong: plan mode builds a plan for you to review.

notes.front: Before Copilot CLI touches a complex, multi-step change, Uma wants it to ask about scope and requirements and propose a plan first. What should she do in her interactive session?
notes.back: B: press Shift+Tab to cycle into plan mode.
notes.explanation: In plan mode Copilot analyses the request, asks clarifying questions and builds a plan before writing any code, which catches misunderstandings early.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Interactive interface”
notes.evidence: Press <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Tab</kbd> to cycle between modes. In plan mode, Copilot analyzes your request, asks clarifying questions to understand scope and requirements, and builds a plan before writing any code. This helps you catch misunderstandings before any code is written, and stay in control of complex, multi-step tasks.
notes.choices:
A) Start it with --allow-all-tools
B) Press Shift+Tab to cycle into plan mode
C) Switch on autopilot mode
D) Prefix the prompt with !
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: it removes approval prompts rather than adding planning. C is wrong: autopilot works without stopping for input. D is wrong: ! runs a shell command without calling the model.

notes.front: When you start Copilot CLI in a folder, what does choosing “Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions” do?
notes.back: It trusts the folder’s files for this and future sessions, so you are not asked again when starting there.
notes.explanation: The docs say to choose it only if it will always be safe for Copilot to work with files in that location.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Using Copilot CLI”
notes.evidence: **2. Yes, and remember this folder for future sessions**: You trust the files in this folder for this and future sessions. You won't be asked again when you start Copilot CLI from this folder. Only choose this option if you are sure that it will always be safe for Copilot to work with files in this location.

notes.front: From which directory do the docs say you should typically not launch Copilot CLI?
notes.back: Your home directory.
notes.explanation: Launching from a directory holding sensitive data, or files you don’t want changed, could expose those files to risk.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Trusted directories”
notes.evidence: Similarly, if you launch the CLI from a directory that contains sensitive or confidential data, or files that you don't want to be changed, you could inadvertently expose those files to risk. Typically, you should not launch Copilot CLI from your home directory.

notes.front: Does GitHub guarantee that files outside trusted directories are protected from Copilot CLI?
notes.back: No. The scoping of permissions is heuristic.
notes.explanation: For that reason the docs point you to their risk mitigation advice.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Trusted directories”
notes.evidence: Scoping of permissions is heuristic and GitHub does not guarantee that all files outside trusted directories will be protected. See [Risk mitigation](#risk-mitigation).

notes.front: Leo has downloaded an unfamiliar project that contains executable files he cannot vouch for. He wants to try Copilot CLI on it. What do the docs advise?
notes.back: B: do not use Copilot CLI in a directory that may contain executables you can’t be sure you trust.
notes.explanation: Trusted directories let Copilot read, modify and execute files, so the docs warn against directories with untrusted executables.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Trusted directories”
notes.evidence: You should only launch Copilot CLI from directories that you trust. You should not use Copilot CLI in directories that may contain executable files you can't be sure you trust.
notes.choices:
A) Launch it there and choose “Yes, and remember this folder”
B) Do not use Copilot CLI in that directory
C) Launch it from his home directory instead
D) Launch it with --allow-all-tools to save time
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: remembering the folder trusts it for future sessions too. C is wrong: the docs say you should typically not launch from your home directory. D is wrong: it lets Copilot run any command without asking.

notes.front: How long does tool-approval option 2, `Yes, and approve TOOL for the rest of the running session`, last?
notes.back: Only for the currently running session; new sessions, or a resumed one, ask again.
notes.explanation: The approval does not carry over, even when you resume the same session later.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Allowed tools”
notes.evidence: **Option 2** allows Copilot to use this tool again, without asking you for permission, for the duration of the currently running session. It will ask for your approval again in new sessions, or if you resume the current session in the future.

notes.front: Choosing approval option 2 for the rm command would let Copilot {{c1::delete any file in the current directory or its subdirectories}} without asking.
notes.back: delete any file in the current directory or its subdirectories
notes.explanation: That is the security implication the docs flag for approving a tool for the rest of the session.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Using Copilot CLI”
notes.evidence: For example, choosing this option for the command `rm` would allow Copilot to delete any file in the current directory or its subdirectories without asking for your approval.

notes.front: What happens when you choose tool-approval option 3, “No, and tell Copilot what to do differently”?
notes.back: Copilot does not run the command; it ends the current operation and waits for your next prompt.
notes.explanation: You can then tell it to continue the task using a different approach.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Using Copilot CLI”
notes.evidence: Copilot will not run the command. Instead, it ends the current operation and awaits your next prompt. You can tell Copilot to continue the task but using a different approach.

notes.front: Ana approves chmod with option 2 during a session, closes the terminal and next day resumes that same session. Copilot wants to run chmod again. What happens?
notes.back: A: Copilot asks for her approval again.
notes.explanation: Option 2 lasts only for the running session; Copilot asks again in new sessions or when you resume one.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Allowed tools”
notes.evidence: It will ask for your approval again in new sessions, or if you resume the current session in the future.
notes.choices:
A) It asks for her approval again
B) It refuses to use chmod ever again
C) It runs chmod with administrator rights
D) It runs chmod without asking, as approved before
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong: option 2 does not carry over into a resumed session. B is wrong: she can simply approve it again. C is wrong: nothing in the approval raises its privileges.

notes.front: What access does Copilot have when you run Copilot CLI with --allow-all-tools?
notes.back: The same access as you to files on your computer; it can run any shell command you can, without asking first.
notes.explanation: The docs flag this with a caution and point to their security considerations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Programmatic interface”
notes.evidence: If you use an automatic approval option such as `--allow-all-tools`, Copilot has the same access as you do to files on your computer, and can run any shell commands that you can run, without getting your prior approval.

notes.front: You run copilot with --allow-all-tools and --deny-tool='shell(rm)'. Can Copilot use rm?
notes.back: No. --deny-tool takes precedence over --allow-all-tools and --allow-tool.
notes.explanation: A deny rule wins even over the broadest allow option.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Allowing tools to be used without manual approval”
notes.evidence: **`--deny-tool`** Prevents Copilot from using a specific tool. This option takes precedence over the `--allow-all-tools` and `--allow-tool` options.

notes.front: How do you stop Copilot CLI from running git push while leaving other git commands alone?
notes.back: `--deny-tool='shell(git push)'`: for git and gh you can name a first-level subcommand.
notes.explanation: Without a subcommand, a rule such as shell(rm) covers every use of that command.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Using the approval options”
notes.evidence: For example, `copilot --deny-tool='shell(rm)'` prevents Copilot from using any `rm` command. For `git` and `gh` commands, you can specify a particular first-level subcommand to allow or deny. For example: ```shell copilot --deny-tool='shell(git push)'

notes.front: Which argument to --allow-tool lets Copilot edit files without individual approval, for tools other than shell commands?
notes.back: `write`, as in `copilot --allow-tool='write'`.
notes.explanation: Shell commands are handled separately, with the shell(COMMAND) argument.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Using the approval options”
notes.evidence: * `'write'` This argument allows or denies tools—other than shell commands—permission to modify files. For example, `copilot --allow-tool='write'` allows Copilot to edit files without your individual approval.

notes.front: Sam wants Copilot CLI to run with every tool allowed except rm and git push. Which command does that?
notes.back: A: `copilot --allow-all-tools --deny-tool='shell(rm)' --deny-tool='shell(git push)'`
notes.explanation: Approval options can be combined, and each --deny-tool overrides the broad allow.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Combining approval options”
notes.evidence: For example, to prevent Copilot from using the `rm` and `git push` commands, but automatically allow all other tools, use: ```shell copilot --allow-all-tools --deny-tool='shell(rm)' --deny-tool='shell(git push)'
notes.choices:
A) copilot --allow-all-tools --deny-tool='shell(rm)' --deny-tool='shell(git push)'
B) copilot --allow-all-tools
C) copilot --yolo --allow-tool='shell(rm)'
D) copilot --deny-tool='shell'
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong: it allows rm and git push too. C is wrong: it allows everything, including rm. D is wrong: it denies every shell command rather than allowing all but two.

notes.front: Which two flags enable all permissions at once in Copilot CLI?
notes.back: --allow-all and --yolo.
notes.explanation: The docs reserve them for situations where you trust Copilot to run freely.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Enable all permissions”
notes.evidence: For situations where you trust Copilot to run freely, you can use the `--allow-all` or `--yolo` flags to enable all permissions at once.

notes.front: What does local sandboxing restrict in Copilot CLI, and how do you turn it on?
notes.back: The commands and tools Copilot runs for you, limiting their filesystem, network and system access; enter /sandbox enable.
notes.explanation: It does not sandbox the CLI itself; with cloud sandboxing, the whole session instead runs remotely in an isolated environment.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Use sandboxing”
notes.evidence: Local sandboxing does not run the CLI itself in a sandbox; instead, the commands and tools that Copilot CLI runs on your behalf are restricted, limiting their access to your filesystem, network, and system capabilities. To enable local sandboxing, enter `/sandbox enable` inside a session. Alternatively, with cloud sandboxing, the entire Copilot CLI session runs remotely in an isolated environment.

notes.front: Raj wants Copilot CLI to look at the contents of src/utils/date.js while answering his question. What is the direct way to include that file in his prompt?
notes.back: C: type @ followed by the file’s relative path, such as @src/utils/date.js.
notes.explanation: Using @ with a relative path adds the file’s contents to the prompt as context for Copilot.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Include a specific file in your prompt”
notes.evidence: To add a specific file to your prompt, use `@` followed by the relative path to the file. For example: `Explain @config/ci/ci-required-checks.yml` or `Fix the bug in @src/app.js`. This adds the contents of the file to your prompt as context for Copilot.
notes.choices:
A) Type #file src/utils/date.js
B) Prefix the path with !
C) Type @src/utils/date.js in the prompt
D) Run /add-dir src/utils
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: #file is a chat variable in Visual Studio Code, not the CLI’s way to add a file. B is wrong: ! runs a shell command without calling the model. D is wrong: /add-dir adds a trusted directory rather than putting a file into the prompt.

notes.front: In a Copilot CLI session, how do you run a shell command directly, without calling the model?
notes.back: Prefix your input with !, for example !git status.
notes.explanation: Skipping the model makes it a quick way to run an ordinary command without leaving the session.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Run shell commands”
notes.evidence: You can prepend your input with `!` to directly run shell commands, without making a call to the model.

notes.front: How do you add a trusted directory by hand during a Copilot CLI session?
notes.back: Use the /add-dir slash command with the directory’s path.
notes.explanation: To switch the working directory altogether without a new session, use /cwd or /cd instead.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Work with files in a different location”
notes.evidence: You can also add a trusted directory manually at any time by using the slash command: ```shell /add-dir /path/to/directory ``` If all of the files you want to work with are in a different location, you can switch the current working directory without starting a new Copilot CLI session by using either the `/cwd` or `/cd` slash commands:

notes.front: How do you stop Copilot CLI while it is still “Thinking” about a prompt?
notes.back: Press Esc twice within half a second.
notes.explanation: The two presses must both come within that half-second window.

notes.front: Besides your prompts and Copilot’s responses, what are two things a Copilot CLI session includes?

notes.front: In Copilot CLI, how do the /every and /after slash commands differ?

notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Using GitHub Copilot CLI”, “Schedule prompts to run later”
notes.evidence: The `/every` command schedules a prompt to run repeatedly, while the `/after` command schedules a one-shot prompt to run once after a specified delay.

notes.front: After a very long Copilot CLI session with several compactions, Copilot cannot recall the exact wording of an error message from the start. Why?
notes.back: C: compaction summarises the history, so fine-grained details such as exact wording may not be kept.
notes.explanation: Compaction is a summarisation process: key points survive, but some detail is inevitably lost.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing context in GitHub Copilot CLI”, “What compaction does not preserve”
notes.evidence: Compaction is a summarization process, so some detail is inevitably lost. The summary captures the key points, but fine-grained details—such as the exact wording of every message, the full output of every command, or minor decisions made early in a long conversation—may not be included.
notes.choices:
A) The session was corrupted and must be deleted
B) Copilot CLI never keeps earlier messages at all
C) Compaction replaced the history with a summary
D) The error message was excluded by a content filter
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: losing fine detail is expected behaviour, not corruption. B is wrong: the summary keeps the key points of earlier work. D is wrong: content filtering is not what removes old detail.

notes.front: When you run Copilot CLI programmatically, how should you grant permissions?
notes.back: Minimally: use --allow-tool and --allow-url to allow only the tools and access the task needs.
notes.explanation: Overly permissive options such as --allow-all should be avoided unless you are working in a sandbox.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Running GitHub Copilot CLI programmatically”, “Tips for using Copilot CLI programmatically”
notes.evidence: **Always give minimal permissions** — use the `--allow-tool=[TOOLS...]` and `--allow-url=[URLs...]` command-line options to give Copilot permission to use only the tools and access that are necessary to complete the task. Avoid using overly permissive options (such as `--allow-all`) unless you are working in a sandbox environment.
